Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Up to now, we've seen several grammatical constructions for implications and biconditionals. In this lesson, we'll review all those that are commonly used.

Content:
The implication [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] has the following grammatical constructions:

Content:
- If [MATH: P,] then [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] only if [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: Q] if [MATH: P]
- [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q]

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] If [MATH: 4 \mid n,] then [MATH: 2 \mid n]

Content:
is equivalent to the following:

Content:
- [MATH: 4 \mid n] implies [MATH: 2 \mid n]
- [MATH: 4 \mid n] only if [MATH: 2 \mid n]
- [MATH: 2 \mid n,] if [MATH: 4 \mid n]

Content:
Using these grammatical constructions correctly within a particular mathematical context can be tricky. It's important to go through each and understand why it's equivalent to [MATH: P\Rightarrow Q.] So, let's do that. We assume that [MATH: P\Rightarrow Q] is true in each case.

Content:
- If [MATH: P,] then [MATH: Q{:}] If [MATH: P] is true, then [MATH: Q] must be true.
- [MATH: P] only if [MATH: Q{:}] The only way that [MATH: P] is true is if [MATH: Q] is also true.
- [MATH: Q] if [MATH: P{:}] [MATH: Q] is guaranteed to be true if [MATH: P] is true.
- [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q.] This is the same as "If [MATH: P,] then [MATH: Q.]"
